passages.title: The Coastal Library · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
The coastal library is a small building near the fishing harbour. Its blue doors face a public garden, and three wide windows look towards the sea. Inside, visitors can find shelves of storybooks, local history books and large-print titles. A ramp beside the main steps provides an alternative entrance for wheelchair users. A reading table stands beside the windows, while a noticeboard near the entrance displays opening hours and weekly activities.

The library opens from eight in the morning until four in the afternoon on weekdays. On Saturday, it closes at noon. The children's corner has floor cushions and a low shelf, while the quiet reading area is located at the back of the building. Visitors can borrow up to three books for two weeks by showing a library card.

The librarian has placed a map near the door to help new visitors find the different areas. The map also shows the nearest bus stop and the public drinking-water point in the garden. It does not include the temporary book table used during special events. The library is more than a place to borrow books: it is also a meeting point for reading groups and local history talks. Its weekly programme changes, so visitors should check the noticeboard for current information.

passages.title: A Day at the Seed Exchange · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
On the first Sunday of September, the village community centre held a seed exchange for local gardeners. The event began at eight thirty in the morning. Volunteers placed labelled envelopes on long tables and prepared a small area where visitors could ask questions about planting seasons. People were invited to bring seeds that had been stored in clean, dry containers.

Mira arrived with her uncle and a packet of bean seeds from their garden. At the entrance, a volunteer asked them to write the plant name and the month when the seeds had been collected. They then visited three tables. One displayed leafy vegetable seeds, another had flowers, and the last contained local fruit varieties. Mira exchanged her beans for two packets of spinach seeds. A gardener explained that the packets should be labelled clearly and stored away from damp places.

By eleven o'clock, the organisers had counted forty-two visitors and recorded thirty-one exchanges. The figures described the event, but they did not show how many seeds would grow successfully. Some visitors took information sheets without exchanging anything. Before leaving, Mira wrote the date on her new packets and thanked the volunteers. She learned that sharing seeds also requires sharing accurate information about their names and storage. The community centre plans another exchange after the next harvest.

passages.title: The Lantern in the Attic · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
When Arman helped his grandmother clear the attic, he found a small paper lantern inside a wooden box. Its red sides were faded, and one corner had been carefully repaired with a strip of green paper. Arman wanted to throw it away because the frame looked weak. His grandmother asked him to wait until she had told him where it came from.

Years earlier, the family had used the lantern during a neighbourhood evening walk. Arman's grandmother had made it with her younger sister, who later moved to another island. The green repair was the sister's work. Each year, the family had kept the lantern in the same box, although nobody had taken it outside for a long time. The grandmother kept a small photograph of the walk in the same box, but she had never written the names on its back. Arman listened quietly. He had assumed the object was only old paper, but it carried a memory that mattered to his grandmother.

They decided not to light the lantern because its paper was dry and fragile. Instead, Arman photographed it and wrote a short label describing its history. His grandmother added the year and the names of the two sisters. They placed the lantern in a clear display case away from direct sunlight. Arman realised that preserving an object does not always mean using it again. Sometimes care means changing how we keep something so that its story can be shared safely. The lantern remained in the attic, but it was no longer an object waiting to be discarded.

passages.title: Making a Simple Rain Gauge · Original A2 Practice Text
passages.text:
A simple rain gauge can help a class compare rainfall on different days. To make one, prepare a clear straight-sided plastic bottle, a ruler, a marker, scissors and a few small stones. The teacher should cut the top from the bottle before the activity. Students must not use sharp tools without adult supervision.

First, place the stones at the bottom of the bottle to keep it steady. Turn the cut top upside down and place it inside the lower part to make a funnel. Use the ruler and marker to draw a scale on the side, starting above the stones. Put the gauge in an open place away from roofs and large trees. Check that it stands upright and cannot easily fall over.

After rainfall, read the water level at the same time each day and write the result in a table. Empty the bottle after recording the measurement. If the gauge moves or fills with leaves, clean it and note the problem in the record. A class can compare measurements from different days, but one homemade gauge may not give perfectly accurate results. Students should use the same location and method each time. The activity is for learning about measurement; it should not be used as an official weather warning system.

passages.title: Why Local Stories Belong in School · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
Schools should include local stories alongside books from other places. Stories about a neighbourhood, a river, a market or a family tradition can help students connect reading with the world they know. They can also introduce different voices and experiences that may be missing from a general textbook.

Local stories offer several learning opportunities. Students can compare how people describe the same place, ask whose perspective is included and investigate how a community has changed. A teacher can guide the discussion by asking students to compare the language and point of view in each account. A story may lead to a history interview, a map-making activity or a discussion about how language changes between generations. Teachers can invite students to bring a family story, but participation should be voluntary because not every learner wishes to share private experiences. A collection can also include public legends and stories contributed with permission.

Some critics worry that local material may take time away from wider literature. This risk can be managed by using local stories as a starting point for comparison rather than as a replacement for other reading. Teachers should check sources, explain when a story has different versions and avoid presenting one family's memory as the only account of an event. The purpose is not to claim that local stories are always more accurate or more important. It is to help students read with curiosity, recognise perspective and understand that literature can reflect many communities. A balanced reading programme can make room for both local and international voices.

passages.title: A Community Mangrove Project · Original B1 Practice Text
passages.text:
A coastal community group has monitored a small mangrove planting project for six months. Volunteers planted seedlings along two sections of a tidal channel after local residents reported that the bank was losing soil during heavy rain. The group marked each planting area and recorded the number of seedlings at the beginning of the project. It also noted the dates of high tides and major storms and recorded broken stems and exposed roots after storms. The team also photographed each section from a marked point so that later visits could use similar views over time.

At the first check, volunteers counted 120 seedlings in the northern section and 100 in the southern section. Six months later, 86 seedlings remained in the northern area and 79 in the southern area. Volunteers replaced some missing markers, but they did not plant new seedlings during the monitoring period. A nearby school helped prepare a sign explaining why the group was collecting data.

The counts show that fewer seedlings were present at the final check than at the beginning. They do not, by themselves, explain why each seedling disappeared or prove that the project has reduced erosion. The team did not measure changes in the channel bank with the same instrument before and after planting, and there was no untreated comparison area. The group plans to continue monitoring and ask a local university for advice on a consistent measurement method. Its report describes survival counts and weather events, while the long-term environmental effect remains uncertain.
